{{Short description|Test for series convergence}}
{{Calculus |Series}}
{{about|the mathematical method of testing for the convergence of an infinite series|the test for determining the flash point of petroleum|Abel test}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Abel's test''' (also known as '''Abel's criterion''') is a method of testing for the [[Convergent series|convergence]] of an [[series (mathematics)|infinite series]]. The test is named after mathematician [[Niels Henrik Abel]], who proved it in 1826.<ref>{{cite journal |first=Niels Henrik |last=Abel |authorlink= Niels Henrik Abel |title=Untersuchungen über die Reihe <math>1+ \frac{m}{x} + \frac{m\cdot (m-1)}{2\cdot 1} x^2 + \frac{m\cdot (m-1)\cdot (m-2)}{3\cdot 2\cdot 1} x^3 + \ldots</math> u.s.w. |journal=[[J. Reine Angew. Math.]] |volume=1 |year=1826 |pages=311–339}}</ref> There are two slightly different versions of Abel's test &ndash; one is used with series of real numbers, and the other is used with [[power series]] in [[complex analysis]]. '''Abel's uniform convergence test''' is a criterion for the [[uniform convergence]] of a [[Series (mathematics)|series]] of [[function (mathematics)|functions]] dependent on [[parameter#Mathematical analysis|parameters]].

== Abel's test in real analysis ==

Suppose the following statements are true:
# <math display=inline>\sum a_n </math> is a convergent series,
# <math>b_n </math> is a monotone sequence, and
# <math>b_n </math> is bounded.
Then <math display=inline>\sum a_nb_n </math> is also convergent.

The test is mainly pertinent and useful in the context of non-absolutely convergent series <math display=inline>\sum a_n</math>.{{cn|date=October 2025}}  It can be proved directly using [[summation by parts]].{{cn|date=October 2025}}

== Abel's test in complex analysis ==
A closely related convergence test, also known as '''Abel's test''', can often be used to establish the convergence of a [[power series]] on the boundary of its [[radius of convergence|circle of convergence]]. Specifically, Abel's test states that if a sequence <math>(a_n)</math> of ''positive real numbers'' is decreasing monotonically with
<math display=block>
\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} a_n = 0,
</math>
then the power series
<math display=block>
f(z) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nz^n
</math>
converges everywhere on the closed [[unit circle]], except possibly at ''z'' = 1. Abel's test cannot be applied when ''z'' = 1, so convergence at that single point must be investigated separately. 

Abel's test implies in particular that the radius of convergence is at least 1. It can also be applied to a power series with radius of convergence ''R'' ≠ 1 by a simple change of variables <math>\zeta = z/R</math>.<ref>(Moretti, 1964, p. 91)</ref> Abel's test is a generalization of the [[alternating series test]], which is the special case ''z'' = −1.

'''Proof of Abel's test:''' Suppose that ''z'' is a point on the unit circle, ''z'' ≠ 1. For each <math>n\geq1</math>, we define

:<math>
f_n(z):=\sum_{k=0}^n a_k z^k.
</math>
By multiplying this function by (1 − ''z''), we obtain
:<math>
\begin{align}
(1-z)f_n(z) & = \sum_{k=0}^n a_k (1-z)z^k   
 = \sum_{k=0}^n a_k z^k - \sum_{k=0}^n a_k z^{k+1}  
 = a_0 + \sum_{k=1}^n a_k z^k - \sum_{k=1}^{n+1} a_{k-1} z^k  \\
& = a_0 - a_n z^{n+1} + \sum_{k=1}^n (a_k - a_{k-1}) z^k .
\end{align}
</math>
The first summand is constant, the second converges uniformly to zero (since by assumption the sequence <math>(a_n)</math> converges to zero). It only remains to show that the series converges. We will show this by showing that it even converges absolutely:
<math>
\sum_{k=1}^\infty \left|(a_k - a_{k-1}) z^k \right| = \sum_{k=1}^\infty |a_k-a_{k-1}|\cdot |z|^k \leq \sum_{k=1}^\infty (a_{k-1}-a_{k})
</math>
where the last sum is a converging telescoping sum. The absolute value vanished because the sequence <math>(a_n)</math> is decreasing by assumption.

Hence, the sequence <math>(1-z)f_n(z)</math> converges (even uniformly) on the closed unit disc. If <math>z\not = 1</math>, we may divide by (1 − ''z'') and obtain the result.

Another way to obtain the result is to apply the [[Dirichlet's test]]. Indeed, for <math>z\ne 1,\ |z|=1</math> holds <math>\left|\sum_{k=0}^n z^k\right|=\left|\frac{z^{n+1}-1}{z-1}\right|\le \frac{2}{|z-1|}</math>, hence the assumptions of the Dirichlet's test are fulfilled.

The following strengthening of the test is also valid: one may replace the condition that <math>(a_n)</math> is decreasing with the condition that it is decreasing for sufficiently large ''n'', that is, that there is some natural number ''m'' for which <math>a_n \geq a_{n+1}</math> whenever ''n'' > ''m''.{{cn|date=October 2025}}

== Abel's uniform convergence test ==
Abel's uniform convergence test is a criterion for the [[uniform convergence]] of a series of functions or an [[improper integral|improper integration]] of functions dependent on [[parameter#Mathematical analysis|parameters]].  It is related to Abel's test for the convergence of an ordinary series of real numbers, and the proof relies on the same technique of [[summation by parts]].

The test is as follows.  Let <math>\{g_n\}</math> be a [[uniformly bounded]] sequence of real-valued [[continuous function]]s on a set <math>E</math> such that <math>g_{n+1}(x) \leq g_n(x)</math> for all <math>x \in E</math> and positive integers <math>n</math>, and let <math>\{f_n\}</math> be a sequence of real-valued functions such that the series <math>\sum f_n(x)</math> converges uniformly on <math>E</math>.  Then <math>\sum f_n(x)g_n(x)</math> converges uniformly on <math>E</math>.
